## The Early Wave: Simulated Teams and Societies

Once LLM calls could be wrapped as stateful tool-using workers, the first LLM multi-agent wave often looked like a small human team: a task was divided into named roles, role-conditioned agents exchanged messages, and their outputs moved through a staged workflow. The working assumption was that this pattern could turn chat models into useful division of labor. If one model could imitate a planner, programmer, critic, or reviewer, perhaps several role-prompted model calls could specialize, check one another, and complete work with less human steering.

There were good reasons to start there. First, roles were cheap control. Chat-tuned LLMs were already good at following persona and task instructions, so "manager," "engineer," "critic," or "scientist" gave a developer a rough behavior policy without training a controller. Second, conversation was the easiest wiring. Before mature agent runtimes, developers could coordinate LLM calls with turn order, messages, summaries, prompt templates, and stop conditions. Third, early benchmarks and demonstrations often tolerated loose coordination. They could reward a better transcript, a more complete prototype, a plausible social simulation, a higher preference judgment, or an executable output without fully isolating whether the gain came from collaboration, extra tokens, more samples, stronger judging, or better prompts.

CAMEL shows this logic clearly. Its AI user, AI assistant, and task-specifier agents used inception prompts, role constraints, message formats, and termination tokens to replace some of the human steering normally needed in chat-based task solving [@camel]. Generative Agents used memory, reflection, and planning to make a society of 25 simulated characters behave believably, which was powerful evidence for social simulation but not the same as reliable task completion [@generativeagents]. ChatDev translated software prototyping into a sequential chat chain of design, coding, review, and testing, while MetaGPT made the same human-team metaphor more structured through standard operating procedures, documents, role-specific subscriptions, and executable feedback [@chatdev; @metagpt]. AutoGen generalized the pattern into conversation programming: agents could be backed by LLMs, humans, tools, code execution, auto-reply functions, and group-chat managers [@autogen]. AgentVerse and AutoAgents extended the same impulse toward recruitment and automatic team construction, while debate systems used multiple model instances as speakers, critics, or judges [@agentverse; @autoagents; @du2023debate; @multiagentdebate; @chateval].

This period had real contributions. It gave researchers and builders a vocabulary for LLM decomposition. It made multi-turn tool use and external state feel natural. It surfaced design dimensions that still matter: role assignment, topology, message passing, memory, tool access, human participation, artifacts, and termination. It also made clear that "agent" is not a single mechanism. In these systems, an agent may be a prompt role, a tool-using controller, a memory-bearing persona, a reviewer, a planner, a software process, or a human proxy.

The weakness was the default causal story. Early systems often implied that roles plus conversation would produce specialization and collective intelligence. Sometimes they did. But the mechanism was often ambiguous. ChatDev and MetaGPT each looked strong under different task suites and metrics; debate results often used more inference and additional judging; CAMEL and Generative Agents were valuable demonstrations but relied on synthetic interaction and subjective or model-assisted evaluation. Was improvement caused by collaboration, or by more tokens, more samples, a stronger final judge, a better prompt, or selection over multiple attempts? Was the team solving a coordination problem, or simply ensembling correlated outputs? Did agent interaction create independent evidence, or did it spread the same error through a longer transcript?

The answer depends on task structure. In open-ended ideation, critique, and proposal generation, role diversity can increase coverage. In tasks with deterministic validators, multiple attempts can be useful if checked independently. In tightly coupled reasoning tasks that fit inside one model context, splitting the work can destroy information and add summarization loss. The durable lesson of 2023 was therefore not that artificial teams solved coordination. It was that LLM workers made coordination easy enough to build and visible enough to study. The next phase of the field had to determine when those teams produced independent evidence, useful checks, and mergeable artifacts, and when they merely spent more inference inside a more convincing transcript.
